headline: Measles hits a 35-year high in America

sources.title: US adds 53 more measles cases to its 2026 total
US highly likely to lose measles elimination status this fall, analysis warns
US measles cases reach 35-year high, for second record-breaking year in a row (video, ABC7)

chunks.text: The United States has [[confirmed]] 2,371 cases of measles in 2026, the worst year since 1991. [[Figures]] that [[health officials]] {{put out}} [[at the end of]] July show 53 new cases in a single week, and the total has already {{gone past}} last year's 2,288, which was itself a [[record]]. Thirty-seven separate [[outbreaks]] have {{cropped up}} in 45 states and [[territories]]. No one has died of measles this year. Three people died in 2025, two of them children.

verbs.wrong: To return to an earlier time

chunks.text: Measles spreads more easily than almost any other disease. If one person has it, [[up to]] [[nine out of ten]] [[unprotected]] people close to them will {{come down with}} it, and the virus can stay in the air of a room for two hours after the patient has left. About 7 percent of this year's patients have {{ended up}} needing [[hospital care]]. Children aged 5 to 19 [[account for]] half of all cases, and children under 5 {{make up}} another [[fifth]].

verbs.correct: To become ill with a disease
verbs.wrong: To fall to a lower level

verbs.correct: To be somewhere in the end

chunks.text: Ninety-three percent of this year's patients had either never been [[vaccinated]] or could not [[prove]] that they had been. Two [[doses]] of the measles vaccine stop the disease 97 percent of the time, but fewer children are getting them. The [[coverage]] rate among [[kindergarten]] children has {{dropped off}}, from 95.2 percent in the 2019 to 2020 school year to 92.5 percent in 2024 to 2025. That now {{falls short of}} the 95 percent that doctors say a community needs to {{hold back}} an outbreak.

verbs.correct: To be less than what is needed
verbs.wrong: To move more slowly than others
To measure a disease every year

chunks.text: The United States {{wiped out}} measles in 2000. That does not mean nobody has caught it since. It means health experts could show that the virus had stopped spreading inside the country [[all year round]], and they call that [[elimination]]. A country keeps that status only as long as the status stays true, and the country loses the status if a single [[chain of infection]] {{carries on}} for more than 12 months. Researchers writing in The Lancet say it is [[highly likely]] the United States will lose its status when a Pan American Health Organization [[committee]] meets in November 2026. Health officials say the way to {{turn around}} the numbers has not changed: two doses of the vaccine, [[on time]], for every child. Without that, a disease the country beat 26 years ago will have {{come back}} to stay.

mainIdea.s: The United States has confirmed 2,371 measles cases in 2026, the worst total since 1991. Most patients were never vaccinated, and the country may soon lose its official elimination status.
mainIdea.why: The article says 93 percent of patients had never been vaccinated and losing elimination status is highly likely this fall.

mainIdea.s: Most of this year's measles patients got sick even after receiving both required doses of the vaccine. Health officials are still urging every family to get both doses on schedule this year.
mainIdea.why: Close, but 93 percent of patients had never been vaccinated, and two doses stop the disease 97 percent of the time.

mainIdea.s: Health officials in Europe say measles cases have been rising sharply across several countries this year. Falling vaccination rates among children are behind much of the rise across the region.
mainIdea.why: This story is about the record measles total in the United States, not about rising cases in Europe.
